t: the positive commandment to rest in the Sabbatical year etc.. Regarding the obligation of this mitzvah in our times see below 10:9.
from working the land. Actions done to the ground.
and working the trees. Actions done to the trees themselves.
he does not receive Torah lashes etc.. For only these four kinds of work are explicit in the verse (Leviticus 25:4-5).
sowing. Which is working the land.
pruning. Zemirah, cutting the branches of the tree to improve it, which is work on the tree.

reaping. Reaping for the sake of working the land (so that more grain will grow; see Hilchot Shabbat 8:4). And below, 4:1, a different prohibition will be discussed, of reaping the crop when done in the usual way (Yad Peshutah).

harvesting. Harvesting grapes for the sake of working the tree (to improve the rest of the fruit). And below, 4:22, a different prohibition will be discussed, of harvesting fruit when done in the usual way (Yad Peshutah).
and the same applies to the vineyard and to other trees. Their law is the same.
and pruning is included in sowing. Since the purpose of pruning is to make fruit grow.
along with the other principal categories not specified in this matter. Such as plowing, which is a principal category of labor regarding Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 7:2).
rabbinic lashes for rebelliousness. Lashes by Rabbinic law.

one who plows or digs. Plowing with a plow drawn by an animal, and digging with a digging tool (Pe'at HaShulchan 20:2); some explain that plowing is of the entire field or a plot, while digging is in a single spot (Derekh Emunah).
one who clears stones. Removes stones from the field.
one who fertilizes. Spreads manure to enrich the soil.
one who layers. Bends a branch attached to a tree and buries it in the ground so that another tree will grow from it.
one who grafts. Inserts a detached branch into another tree so that it will fuse with it and grow.
the blemishes. Defects that develop in the tree.
and he may not strip off dry leaves and branches. He may not remove dry leaves or branches from the tree.
and he may not dust its foliage with dust. He may not scatter dust on it for the tree's benefit (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 2:2).
and he may not smoke it. He may not produce smoke.
with something that has a foul odor. A foul smell that drives away animals.
and he may not smear the unripe figs or pierce them. In order to hasten their ripening.
and he may not bind the saplings. He may not tie their branches upward (ibid. 2:4).
and he may not trim them. He may not cut off the tops of the branches, and likewise he may not scatter ash for the tree's benefit (ibid.).
and he may not cut back. "Yefasseg" is like "yefassek" (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Parah 11:9): he may not cut from the trees for the sake of renewed growth.
a thicket of reeds. A tangle of reed plants.
because it is working the ground. For he burns them to prepare the ground for sowing.
and one does not train a cow to plow except on sand. When training it for plowing, one does so in a place not fit for sowing, where he does not look like he is plowing.
and one does not test seeds. To see whether they are good.
in a pot full of earth. Since sometimes one sows in a pot, and he would look like he is sowing.
but one may test them in a pot full of dung. Animal droppings, for it is not customary to sow in such a pot.
and one may soak seeds in the Sabbatical year etc.. Because this soaking is not working the ground.

and one may keep aloe etc.. Aloe is a shrub with fleshy leaves, grown for ornament and medicine (aloe vera). The Kesef Mishneh explained that one may maintain it in the Sabbatical year, unlike other tender vegetables that grew on their own (below 4:18), because aloe usually grows by itself and no suspicion will arise that it was sown in the Sabbatical year, but watering it is forbidden because of this suspicion. Others explained that one may maintain it, meaning care for it in the permitted manner during the Sabbatical year, but not water it, since it can survive without watering, for its leaves are fleshy and store water (Rabbi Y. Felix on the Jerusalem Talmud, pp. 254-255).
one marks the tree with red dye. One marks it in red so that those who see it will pray for it not to shed its fruit (Babylonian Talmud Shabbat 67a).

and one loads it with stones. A tree that sheds its fruit because of excess richness and strength, one weakens its vigor by loading stones on it, thereby preventing the fruit from falling (Babylonian Talmud and Rashi there).
and they hoe. They hoe (this is also the reading in some versions).
and the one who loosens the soil. The hoer.
to improve. To enhance.
the cracks. The fissures in the wood.

if they were farther apart than ten to a beit se'ah. If the trees are planted at great distances, so that ten trees are spread over an area larger than a beit se'ah, which is an area suitable for sowing a se'ah of wheat (fifty cubits square, about 625 square meters).
they draw water from tree to tree. By means of channels.

the white soil. The portion of an orchard field that is suitable for sowing grain and legumes, where the trees are planted at great distances, according to the measure given at the start of the halakhah (Commentary on the Mishnah, Mo'ed Katan 2:10, and see also Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 2:1).
they sprinkle it with water. They drip a little water on it (but regular watering is forbidden, as stated at the start of the halakhah).
basins for vines. Hollows to collect water beneath the vines.
and they make the water channel at the outset. They dig a water channel.
the pools. Large hollows for collecting water, from which water is taken to water the trees.
as we explained. Above, halakhah 2.
plowed it. Turned over its soil.
and he may not sow it at the end of the Sabbatical year. In the entire year following the Sabbatical year.
and one may not lease it from him etc.. The Sages also forbade another person to sow it, if the field's owner receives a share of the crop.
and if he died, his son may sow it. For the son did not commit a prohibition, and there is no reason to penalize him (and compare below 3:11).
they did not penalize him. Since his actions in the Sabbatical year did not help prepare the ground for sowing, but only the plowing before sowing.
if some of the leaves were exposed, he need not worry. For that is the way of storing, not of sowing, and he does not want them to take root (Hilchot Kilayim 2:11).
the lof. A kind of onion.

it must not be less than four kavs, at a height of a handbreadth, with a handbreadth of earth over it. The Sages required that a large quantity of lof (four kavs) be buried together in a concentrated pile (a handbreadth high) and covered with a handbreadth of earth, for burying in this fashion does not look like sowing.
to stir. To mix with water the soil in which rice grows (which was sown in the sixth year), in order to maintain its moisture, because this is vital for the rice to survive.
but he may not trim. He may not trim the rice leaves.
a person may gather wood and stones etc.. If he needs the wood and stones.
the large ones. The large pieces of wood and stones.
so that he not say to him, "see what a favor etc.". For if he says this it is evident that he wants his fellow's field improved so that his fellow will return the favor.
for his animal testifies about him... his hired worker testifies about him. That he needs the grass or wood, and does not intend to improve the ground.
for wood. For the use of the wood.
it is permitted to uproot. To pull out the trees with their roots, even though his actions make the ground fit for sowing.
he cut down three... he may not uproot, for he is improving the land. For the size of the area of three trees is suitable for sowing (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 4:4).
from the ground. Close to the ground.
one who splits an olive tree. Cuts branches from it.
because it is work. For he improves the tree.
but he may cover with stones or straw. To prevent the tree from drying out.
one who trims the tails of vines. Cuts off their tails.
he may cut as is his way. If he needs the thing that is cut, and does not intend to improve the tree.
with an axe. A hatchet.
and with a saw. A kind of saw.
a virgin sycamore. A sycamore is a wild fig species; it is called virgin in its first growth, when it has never yet been cut.
not so that it will grow. Not in order to graft it anew.
but that it not split further. To split more.
that was cracked. That was split and cleft.
fertilizers. Organic waste that helps fertilize the ground, such as animal droppings or fruit peels.

and if he took out and set up a rubbish heap from it, it is permitted. If he designated a certain place for the manure where he piles it, he may take it out, since he does not look like one who is fertilizing, provided he observes the conditions later in the halakhah.

once it begins to form. Once it begins to ripen (and perhaps it means when its ripening is complete; see Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 3:1 in the various translations), and a sort of protrusions form on it.
the mattik. The bitter fruit of the colocynth plant, called "mattik" in euphemistic language (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
from one hundred fifty se'ah. About 1050 liters.
if he had a small amount. If he had a little manure in his field before the Sabbatical year (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 3:3).
he may keep adding to it. And he need not remove much at once.
and he may not make more than three rubbish heaps in each beit se'ah. For spreading manure in many places looks like fertilizing.
beit se'ah. See above 1:8.
three heaps of rubbish in each beit se'ah. Three piles of rubbish in each beit se'ah, and each pile has at least one hundred fifty se'ah of manure.
storehouse. One large pile with no limit on quantity.
or if he dug three handbreadths into the ground and set the manure in a heap. In such a way that the digging remains evident even after he placed the pile of manure in it (Yad Peshutah).
for the gathering of manure. For collecting the manure.
the sheep pen. A fenced place for gathering the flock.

in the way of all who gather manure. Under the conditions mentioned in the earlier halakhot, for the law of moving manure from the pen to the field is like the law of moving it from the courtyard to the field.

and one who makes a pen in his field in the Sabbatical year. In order to fertilize his field (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 3:4); they permitted this because he does not fertilize by hand, but the fertilizing happens by itself through the flock (Rabbi Y. Kafih and others). Some infer from the Rambam's wording here that the permission applies only when his intent is for the sake of the flock and not for fertilizing the field (Radbaz, Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 19:13, Rabbi Y. Kafih; and see Rabbi Avraham ben David).
beit sa'atayim. Fifty cubits by one hundred cubits (about 1200 square meters).
he leaves one wall of the pen's walls. He takes three walls out of the four walls of the pen, and leaves one wall in place.
and makes another pen beside it. By moving the three walls he removed to the other side of the wall that remained.
he leaves some of it. He leaves a small place in it unfertilized, as a reminder.
a person may not open a quarry etc.. He may not begin to quarry stones from a large rock in his field.
to improve his field. For sowing.
and split. Broke up, quarried.
twenty-seven stones in a square of three by three by a height of three. A square of three stones by three stones, which is nine stones, all of this multiplied by three layers.
each stone of them a cubit etc.. Large stones that are generally used for building.
at a height of a cubit. A cubit high.
it is permitted etc.. Provided that he does not intend to improve his field (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 3:5).
to quarry out. To hew out.
each one of them the load of two. Carried by two people together because of its weight.
for he takes it for the sake of the stones. For it is not customary to clear away a fence in order to sow in its place, and the stones themselves are also heavy and suitable for building.
it was less than ten. Handbreadths, so it is not considered a fence.

where he intended to improve his field. Where he takes the fence for the sake of using the stones as explained in the previous halakhah, and at the same time it is convenient for him that the place of the fence be improved for sowing after the Sabbatical year.
and he dismantles. He takes apart the fence (some versions read: "gorid" or "gomem," and see Rambam Meduyak by Rabbi Y. Shilat, that perhaps it should read "godeid").

even though he is a contractor. Who received the field to work for a share of the crop, nevertheless his law is that of a stranger with no interest in improving the field for sowing, since it is not known whether the field will be under his responsibility the next year as well.
stones that are fit etc.. That are not embedded deep in the ground.
two of the load of two each. Two heavy stones, each carried by two people, and which are therefore fit for building.
a heap of pebbles. A pile of small stones.
and if there is rock or straw beneath them etc.. Because everyone sees that he does not intend to sow.

a person may not fill a ravine etc.. A ravine is a slope that is customarily made fit for sowing by building retaining walls of stones (terraces) and filling the resulting space with earth. In the Sabbatical year it is forbidden to fill the area with earth, but the walls themselves, made of stones, may be built.

and any stone that he can... it may be taken. But a stone that he can take only by going down into the ravine, it is forbidden to take, since he looks like one improving his field for sowing (Commentary on the Mishnah and Rash, Shevi'it 3:8).
it is permitted to bring them from anywhere. Because they are used for building.
and likewise the contractor brings etc.. One who receives a field to work may bring stones from it; see above halakhah 8 for explanation.
a breach that is closed with earth. A stone fence between his field and the public domain that was breached, and in the place of the breach there is a mound of earth blocking it.
it is forbidden to build it. For he looks like one improving the field for sowing (Rivak"o and Radbaz).
or if it was not closed with earth... it is permitted to build it. For his intent is only to guard the field.

it is forbidden for him to build a fence in the Sabbatical year between his field and his neighbor's field. Since there is no great need for it, it appears that his intent is to prepare the field for sowing.
and it is permitted to deepen. In his digging for the sake of the fence.
in the way of all who pile manure. That is, he piles the earth as manure is piled in the Sabbatical year (above halakhot 1-3).
a pit, a trench, and a cave. Various forms of water reservoirs.
he piles the earth in his field in the way of all diggers. That is, they pile the earth in the manner of piling manure, so that he will not look like one improving the field.
a halakhah to Moshe from Sinai that it is forbidden. The mitzvah of this extension is not written explicitly in the Torah, but was transmitted by tradition.
when the Temple stands, it was forbidden by oral tradition. It is the tradition of the Sages that it was forbidden only in the time of the Temple.
Atzeret. The festival of Shavuot.
and the white field. A field designated for growing grain and legumes.
until Passover. For plowing after Passover no longer benefits the sixth-year grain, but prepares the ground for the Sabbatical year, and similarly for plowing an orchard field after Shavuot.
every three trees to a beit se'ah. In an area of a beit se'ah (see above 1:8) at least three trees are planted.
a barren tree. One that does not bear fruit.

they regard them as though they were figs, if they are fit to produce etc.. They estimate according to the size of the trees and the abundance of their branches how much fruit they would produce if they were fig trees.
if they are fit to produce. The three of them together (Rivak"o, and so it is implied in Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 1:4).
a cake of pressed figs. Pressed figs stuck together in the shape of a loaf of bread.
of sixty manah. Weighing sixty manah.

so that the cattle etc.. A yoke of oxen, which is a distance of four cubits (Babylonian Talmud Bava Batra 83a), for that is the way of planting trees, and if there is not that distance between them they will eventually be uprooted.

and one is fit to produce... and the two are not fit to produce a se'ah. It may mean that each one separately is not fit to produce a se'ah, which is about a third of the measure of sixty manah. For each of the trees must be fit to produce a third of sixty manah (according to the Ra'avad in his glosses and Shenot Eliyahu, Shevi'it 1:4). In most versions the word "se'ah" is missing, and according to this it may be sufficient that each tree be fit to produce any amount of the measure, provided the three together produce sixty manah (Rivak"o).

one plows for them only as much as they need etc.. Around the tree, in the place where the fig picker stands (the "orah") and where the fig basket is set beside it, one plows until Shavuot, and in the rest of the area until Passover.

even though some of them are not fit to produce. For if there are more than three trees, it is not necessary that each of them be fit to produce a part of sixty manah, but it suffices that three are fit.
until Rosh HaShanah. Of the Sabbatical year, since young saplings have not yet grown strong enough, and without this plowing they would spoil (Radbaz).
surrounded in a crown. Planted in a semicircle (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevi'it 1:6), and not scattered over the whole area.
but only as much as they need. Around the sapling to the full extent of the orah and its basket, and it is permitted to plow there until Rosh HaShanah (Derekh Emunah).
and it put forth replacements. It began to grow again.
and all these matters in the time of the Temple as we said. Above, halakhah 1.
the cucumber beds. A place where cucumbers are sown.
and the gourd beds. A place where gourds are sown.
and a beit hashelahin. A field needing constant irrigation (above 1:8).
and they fertilize, strip, dust, and smoke. Actions that benefit the tree (see in detail above 1:5 and the explanation there).
and they nibble, prune, and trim. Removing unwanted branches and parts of the tree.
and they apply foul odors to the saplings, bind them, and trim them. To protect the young trees (see above 1:5 and the explanation there).
and they make houses for them. Shelters to protect from rain or sun.
and they smear the unripe figs and pierce them. See above 1:5 and the explanation there.

unripe figs of the eve of the Sabbatical year that entered the Sabbatical year... one does not smear etc.. Fruits that did not finish ripening before the Sabbatical year may not be smeared or pierced in the Sabbatical year to hasten their ripening, because of the prohibition of work in the Sabbatical year.
and those of the Sabbatical year that went out into the end of the Sabbatical year, one does not smear etc.. Because the sanctity of the Sabbatical year applies to them.
on the slopes of the ravines. On the slopes of the mountains (see above 2:11 for this law in the Sabbatical year itself).
they graft... they layer. See above 1:4.
that the sapling take hold. That its roots spread in the ground.
two weeks. Two weeks, so that the permission to plant applies when at least forty-four days remain until Rosh HaShanah (until the fifteenth of Av).

lest an observer say, "they were planted in the Sabbatical year". For when one plants after this time, the years of orlah are counted from the following year (Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 9:8-10), and one who sees that the count of years begins from the Sabbatical year might think that planting in the Sabbatical year is permitted.
they require the heir to uproot. Because the concern "lest an observer say..." still exists (and compare above 1:13).
roots that were cut earlier and sprouted again. Plant roots that remained in the ground after the plant was cut, and grew again in the Sabbatical year.
sefiach. Appendages to the main crop.
that came up on their own and have no seed. For their way is to grow by themselves without human sowing.
that was well worked. That was plowed thoroughly.
and set up a heap. A large pile of grain.
and threshed with cattle. Separated the kernels from the ears by means of oxen dragging a threshing implement.
who reaped for the sake of working the land. So that the ground will produce better afterward.
as we explained. Above 1:1-2.
and beats. Separates the kernels by beating with a stick.
and by Rabbinic law. A decree of the Sages.
grain. The five species of grain (Hilchot Kilayim 1:8).
and legumes. Seeds that are human food, such as peas and rice (ibid.).
and garden seeds. Seeds of which one eats only the fruit without the seed, such as onion and other vegetables (ibid.).
fruits of trees. About which they did not worry regarding transgressors, since usually a tree that yields ripe fruit in the Sabbatical year was planted before the Sabbatical year.
the peigam. A wild plant with a sharp smell and yellow flowers.
and the yarbuzin. Kinds of asparagus.
the wild ones. That grow wild.
rabbinic lashes for rebelliousness. Lashes by Rabbinic law.
in an unplowed field. A field that was not plowed.
and in a plowed field. A field that was plowed but not sown.
a person does not turn his attention there. He does not invest his time in caring for it.
and a plowed field, he wants its improvement. To sow it at the proper time and in an orderly fashion.

and a vineyard field does not prohibit his vineyard. For one who sows grain or vegetables next to vines prohibits both for benefit because of kilayim of the vineyard (Hilchot Kilayim 5:7). And even though one who sows his vineyard in the Sabbatical year does not prohibit it (ibid. 5:8), people are nevertheless accustomed not to sow in a vineyard (Chazon Ish, Kilayim 3:29).
the straw. The waste of the grain, which is unfit for human food.
and they did not decree against it. For there is no concern that a person will sow for the sake of the straw.
that went out into the end of the Sabbatical year. That were not harvested until the eighth year.
are forbidden to eat. Lest he sow at the end of the Sabbatical year for the beginning of the eighth.

and one does not pull them up by hand, but plows as usual etc.. Some explained that it means that one may not pull them up by hand since their picking is forbidden (above halakhah 3), but one may plow and let the animal graze as usual, and there is no concern either about using sefiach as fertilizer for his field, or lest they sprout again (Yad Peshutah, Torat HaShemitah, pp. 561-562, see there; and see Chazon Ish, Shevi'it 9:6, who explained it otherwise).

and from Chanukah onward sefiach is permitted. Since produce sown in the eighth year is commonly found in the market, and there is no concern that a person will sow at the end of the Sabbatical year for this time. However, when it is known of a certain species that it is found in the market at an earlier time, it is permitted from that time, as explained in the next halakhah (Derekh Emunah, Yad Peshutah).
the grown ones are permitted. Since even the land that may be sown in the eighth year helps in their growth (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:14).
onions that went out of the Sabbatical year into the end of the Sabbatical year. And were harvested in the eighth year.
if similar ones have been produced. If onions that were sown in the eighth year have already grown.
and so with the other fruits. Fruits of the ground.
one may buy. Purchase.
at the end of the Sabbatical year. In the eighth year.
if the early fruit ripened. If the first fruits of the eighth year ripened.
the late ones are permitted. It is permitted to eat of the Sabbatical year's fruits that remained and were late to ripen.
